## Does Hypnosis Help with Smoking Cessation? The Evidence

Your instinct is largely supported by the highest-quality evidence available, though the picture is nuanced rather than a flat "no."

**The strongest evidence: uncertain/insufficient.** The Cochrane systematic review of hypnotherapy for smoking cessation—the gold-standard synthesis of randomized controlled trials—concludes there is insufficient evidence to determine whether hypnotherapy is more effective than other treatments (like counseling) or no treatment at all for helping people quit smoking long-term. This is due to small trial sizes, high risk of bias, and inconsistent results across studies (https://ora.ox.ac.uk/objects/uuid:f8ad59f1-8e99-47f0-adfc-79e6b149e6a4/files/rtb09j577m).

A 2021 Cochrane umbrella review reaffirmed this uncertainty, noting that even after considering newer studies, confidence in hypnosis's effectiveness for smoking cessation remains low (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2024.1330362/full).

The National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH), a U.S. government authority, echoes this conclusion, stating current evidence does not clearly show hypnotherapy is effective for quitting smoking, unlike counseling or medication, which reliably double or triple quit rates (https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/providers/digest/complementary-health-approaches-for-smoking-cessation).

**Evidence on the other side.** Not all research is negative. A 2025 systematic review (Ekanayake & Elkins) took a broader approach, examining 63 studies from 1968–2022, and reported more favorable findings for hypnosis as a cessation aid—though this review used looser inclusion criteria than Cochrane's strict RCT standard (https://www.ishhypnosis.org/encyclopedia/the-potential-benefit-of-hypnosis-for-smoking-cessation/).

**Conclusion:** Based on the most rigorous evidence (Cochrane, NCCIH), the answer leans toward "no clear proof it works better than other methods"—it's not that hypnosis definitely fails, but that quality evidence hasn't established it as effective. Evidence-based options like counseling and medication remain far better supported.
